<reason>Side A built a stronger path to victory by demonstrating that capping international recruitment fails to create family-suitable housing (freeing only student rooms that locals often cannot use), harms domestic students through lost tuition cross-subsidies, and arbitrarily discriminates by nationality when universities equally control domestic enrollment growth. A's "beds-first" alternative—conditioning all admissions on secured accommodation—directly addresses housing pressure immediately without sacrificing revenue or targeting foreigners, effectively neutralizing B's immediacy advantage. While B made compelling points about institutional externalities and the discretionary nature of international recruitment, A's rebuttals exposed vagueness in B's trigger mechanisms and B suffered execution costs from clipped speeches (Turns 3 and 9), preventing full crystallization of their case.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 8) was decisive: answering the pressure questions with the "conditional admission" proposal (no enrollment without contracted beds) which operates on the same admissions cycle as a cap yet preserves revenue and targets the actual housing bottleneck, while exposing that B's vacancy-rate trigger could persist for years in severe shortages, effectively converting the "temporary brake" into an indefinite revenue cut.</best_rebuttal>
